_meta: A set of questions, each answered several times by a model at temperature, used to show that majority-vote (self-consistency) accuracy over k samples is a different and usually higher number than the accuracy of a single sample -- so reporting one while deploying the other misstates the system, and to show the limit: majority vote rescues a question only when the correct answer is the plurality, and cannot fix one the model is systematically wrong about. For a task with a verifiable answer, sampling the model once gives an answer that is right with some probability; sampling it k times and taking the answer that appears most often (self-consistency) aggregates those samples. When the model's probability mass concentrates on the correct answer while its errors scatter across many different wrong answers, the correct answer is the plurality even on questions where a single sample is more often wrong than right, so majority vote beats single-sample accuracy. But when the model is systematically wrong -- most samples give the same wrong answer -- the plurality is that wrong answer, and no amount of voting recovers the truth. On this fixture four questions each have five sampled answers with gold answer A: the mean single-sample accuracy is 0.45 while the majority-vote accuracy is 0.75; one question is rescued by voting although only 40% of its individual samples are correct, and one question has a wrong majority (three of five samples agree on B) that voting cannot fix. The gold answers and the sampled answers per question are the fixture; the per-question single-sample accuracy, the mean single-sample accuracy, the majority answer, and the majority-vote accuracy are computed. Stdlib only.
